## Answer: $\tfrac{1}{10}$

**Step 1: $T_2(P_n)$ is an induced subgraph of the square grid.** Identify the vertex $\{i,j\}$ with $i<j$ with the lattice point $(i,j)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$. Two vertices are adjacent exactly when one token moves one step along the path, i.e. $(i,j)\sim(i\pm1,j)$ or $(i,j)\sim(i,j\pm1)$, provided both endpoints stay in the triangle $\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n\}$. So $T_2(P_n)$ is the subgraph of the grid induced on this triangle.

**Step 2: Lower bound.** The maximum degree is at most 4, so each vertex dominates at most 5 vertices (itself plus at most 4 neighbours). With $|V| = \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n^2-n}{2}$,
$$\gamma(T_2(P_n)) \ge \frac{|V|}{5} = \frac{n^2-n}{10}.$$

**Step 3: Upper bound.** The infinite grid has a perfect dominating set of density $1/5$, given by the points $(i,j)$ with $i+2j\equiv 0 \pmod 5$. Restrict this set to the triangle. Every interior vertex of the triangle is dominated by a pattern point, either inside the triangle or on one of its neighbouring cells just outside. Only vertices near the boundary, $O(n)$ of them, can be left undominated. Adding one dominator for each such vertex gives
$$\gamma(T_2(P_n)) \le \frac{n^2}{10} + O(n).$$

**Step 4: Conclude.** Combining the two bounds, $\gamma(T_2(P_n)) = \frac{n^2}{10} + O(n)$, so
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\gamma(T_2(P_n))}{n^2} = \frac{1}{10}.$$

ANSWER: 1/10
